svg.text: AIRWAY PROCEDURES: SIZE IT, TIME IT, WATCH THE PATIENT
Every one of these harms if it is too big, too long or done to the wrong patient.

g.text: Size from the incisors to the
angle of the jaw.
Too long presses the epiglottis shut. Too short pushes the tongue back.

svg.text: ONLY IF THE GAG IS ABSENT

g.text: An oropharyngeal airway in a patient
who still has a gag reflex provokes
vomiting, and the airway you were
protecting fills with gastric contents.
If she resists it, she does not need it.
Pre-oxygenate. Insert with no suction
applied. Apply it only on withdrawal.
Ten to fifteen seconds at most, then
let the patient recover before repeating.
Suction removes oxygen along with secretions.
Two spare tubes: the same size and one
smaller. Tracheal dilators. Suction, ready
and tested. Saline and syringe.
A tube that comes out at three in the morning
cannot wait for someone to fetch a set.
Position the affected segment uppermost so gravity drains it towards the larger airways, then let the
patient cough. Do it before meals or two hours after, never straight after eating.
Stop for breathlessness, pain, haemoptysis or a falling saturation. The treatment must not cost more than it gives.
